title: Intervals and bit tricks in Python (bisect, bit_count, masks)
seriesDescription: Shortest paths, union-find, tries, intervals, bits, dynamic programming, greedy and backtracking with Python code. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function merge(intervals) that merges all overlapping closed intervals (touching intervals like [1,2] and [2,3] also merge) and returns a sorted list of [start, end] lists.
questions.explanation: sorted(...) returns a new list, so the caller's input is untouched; append a fresh [s, e] so output lists do not alias the input. Time O(n log n). Other valid approaches exist, such as keeping the current start and end in local variables.

checks.label: sorts by the start value
extends the last interval using max of the ends
starts a new interval when the next one begins after the last end
returns the merged list

questions.prompt: Write a Python function min_rooms(meetings) where meetings is a list of [start, end] pairs. Return the minimum number of rooms using a min-heap of end times. A meeting that starts exactly when another ends can reuse the room.
questions.explanation: The heap size at the end equals the peak number of rooms, since a room is only added when none is free. A sweep line over sorted starts and ends is an equally good O(n log n) solution. For [[0,5],[5,10]] the answer is 1 because of the <= test.

checks.label: sorts the meetings by start time
uses heapq push and pop on end times
frees a room when the earliest end is <= the new start
returns the heap size

questions.prompt: Write a Python function in_subnet(ip, network, prefix_len) that returns True if the 32-bit IPv4 address ip (a non-negative int) belongs to the CIDR block network/prefix_len, using bit operations and no ipaddress module. It must also work for prefix_len == 0.
questions.explanation: Python ints are unbounded, so the shifted mask must be cut back to 32 bits with & 0xFFFFFFFF. For prefix_len = 0 the shift gives 0 after masking, so no special case is needed. ip >> (32 - p) == network >> (32 - p) is an equally good form.

checks.label: builds a mask from 32 - prefix_len
keeps the mask within 32 bits (& 0xFFFFFFFF or a complement of host bits)
applies the mask with &
compares the masked values for equality

questions.prompt: Write a Python function popcount(n) for n >= 0 that counts the set bits using the n & (n - 1) trick, without bin() or int.bit_count().
questions.explanation: Runs in O(number of set bits). In real code use n.bit_count() (Python 3.10+). For negative Python ints this loop would never end, because ints are unbounded; mask first with & 0xFFFFFFFF.

checks.label: clears the lowest set bit with n & (n - 1)

questions.prompt: Write a Python class MyCalendar with book(start, end) for half-open events [start, end). It returns False (and stores nothing) if the new event overlaps an existing one, else stores it and returns True. Keep a sorted list and use the bisect module.
questions.explanation: Only the neighbours can collide, so the search is O(log n); the list insert is O(n) in the worst case but very fast in practice. Half-open intervals let [10,20) and [20,30) coexist.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function missing_number(nums) for a list holding n distinct numbers taken from 0..n with one missing; return the missing one in O(n) time and O(1) extra space using XOR or a sum.
questions.explanation: XOR of 0..n with every element cancels all pairs and leaves the missing number. n(n+1)/2 - sum(nums) is the equally valid sum version, and Python ints never overflow. Sorting or a hash set would use more time or space.

checks.label: uses the length of the list as n
combines values with XOR or a sum
returns the result

questions.prompt: 1000 in binary is 1111101000. What does (1000).bit_count() return?
questions.explanation: Ones in 1111101000: five in a row plus one more = 6. int.bit_count() needs Python 3.10+; older code uses bin(n).count('1').
1000 is 1111101000 in binary, which is 10 digits. bit_length is the position of the highest set bit, so it equals floor(log2(n)) + 1 for n > 0.

questions.prompt: What does ~5 evaluate to in Python?
questions.explanation: ~x equals -x - 1 because Python ints behave like infinite two's complement, so ~5 = -6. Using ~x to flip only 8 bits needs a mask: ~5 & 0xFF = 250.

questions.prompt: What does (-1 & 0xFFFFFFFF) >> 28 evaluate to in Python?
questions.explanation: Masking -1 with 0xFFFFFFFF gives 4294967295, the 32-bit unsigned view with 32 ones. Shifting right by 28 leaves the top 4 bits, 1111 = 15. Python has no unsigned shift operator, so you mask first.
Parenthesising is still good style for readers. The same-looking line misparses in some other languages, so do not rely on it in a mixed codebase.

options.why: Correct: in Python the bitwise operators rank above the comparisons.

options.text: As n & ((n - 1) == 0), which raises a TypeError for most n.
options.why: That grouping would need == to bind tighter than &, which it does not in Python.

options.text: As a chained comparison n & (n - 1) and (n - 1) == 0.
options.why: Chaining applies only to comparison operators such as a < b == c, not to &.

options.text: Python rejects the line with a SyntaxError until it is parenthesised.
options.why: The expression is valid syntax, so Python simply evaluates it.

questions.prompt: A negative Python int x must be read as its unsigned 32-bit value, for example -1 as 4294967295. Which expression does that?
questions.explanation: This mask is the Python replacement for unsigned shifts and overflow wrapping. Combine it with >> to emulate unsigned shifts.

options.why: Correct: masking keeps the low 32 bits of the infinite two's complement form.

options.text: x >>> 0, an unsigned shift of x by zero bits
options.why: Python has no >>> operator, so this is a syntax error.

options.text: abs(x), the absolute value of x
options.why: abs(-1) is 1, which is not the 32-bit pattern of -1.
A remainder by 31 has no relation to the 32-bit pattern.

questions.explanation: Mask first when you want an unsigned shift: (-1 & 0xFFFFFFFF) >> 28 == 15.
questions.reason: The >> operator on a negative int fills the vacated bits with zeros.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: >> on Python ints is an arithmetic shift that keeps the sign, so the result stays -1; R is false because it does not fill with zeros.

questions.assertion: (ip & mask) == (network & mask) tests whether ip is in the block network/prefix_len.
questions.reason: The mask zeroes the host bits, so only the network bits are compared.

whys.a: Right: R describes what the mask does, which is exactly why the comparison works.
whys.b: R is the explanation, not a side fact.

questions.prompt: Preparing intervals for a merge in Python.
questions.explanation: Both lists and tuples compare element by element, so no key function is needed for start-then-end order.
questions.assertion: sorted(intervals) on a list of [start, end] lists orders them by start, then by end.
questions.reason: sorted returns a new list and leaves the input list unchanged.

whys.a: Returning a new list is not why lists order by start first; lexicographic comparison is.
whys.b: Right: both are true, but they are independent facts: ordering comes from comparing lists element by element.

questions.prompt: Complete the recurrence that counts the set bits of every number from 0 to n in O(n) with a list bits.
questions.explanation: This is LeetCode 338 (Counting Bits). The answer for i reuses an already computed smaller number, so it is a DP over bits; i & (i - 1) works too: bits[i] = bits[i & (i - 1)] + 1.
questions.text: With bits[0] = {1}, use bits[i] = bits[i {2} 1] + (i {3} 1): drop the lowest bit, then add it back if it was set.
